pentapeptide-18.summary: A topical peptide sold as Leuphasyl to soften expression lines on the forehead and around the eyes.

quick.overview:
Pentapeptide-18 is a short cosmetic peptide marketed as Leuphasyl, often described as a topical 'Botox-like' ingredient. People use it to soften expression lines on the forehead and around the eyes.

It is described as an enkephalin mimic that binds receptors at nerve endings, closes calcium channels and reduces acetylcholine release, so the muscles beneath expression lines receive less contraction signalling. The cited papers did not test this directly in skin. A 2024 study of a retinol-and-pentapeptide-18 eye cream reported wrinkle-area reductions in 20 women; the cream also contained retinol, so the peptide's share of the result is not separated out.
quick.how: It is used in creams and eye products applied to expression-line areas, usually alongside other actives such as retinol. Cosmetic use is a daily routine, and visible smoothing in studies of combination creams is assessed over weeks.
quick.risks: No peptide-specific adverse events were reported in the sources. The retinol in the studied cream was linked to extra peeling. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Used in creams to soften expression lines on the forehead and around the eyes. It is described as dampening nerve-to-muscle signalling, so lines from repeated contraction look smoother. The human data come from a retinol-and-peptide eye cream.

pentapeptide-3.summary: A cosmetic peptide name that has meant the collagen-signalling KTTKS (Matrixyl) and is also tied to Vialox, used for smoother, less lined skin.

quick.overview:
Pentapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide name people use in anti-aging products for smoother, less lined skin. The name has referred to different peptides: before 2006 it denoted palmitoyl KTTKS (Matrixyl), and it is also tied to the Vialox brand, sold as a muscle-relaxing 'Botox-like' ingredient.

KTTKS-type peptides are described as matrikines that signal skin cells to make collagen and other matrix proteins, which is the route to firmer, smoother-looking skin. Research on the family is mostly in cultured cells, and a 2019 study of 32 KTTKS analogues found none cytotoxic to fibroblasts. Suppliers describe Vialox as reducing muscle signalling; no clinical study of a Vialox product was found.
quick.how: It is applied in serums and creams as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Because the name is ambiguous, users check the full ingredient name on the label to see which peptide is meant.
quick.risks: No adverse events were reported in the sources. It is a cosmetic ingredient.

angle.text: Applied for smoother, less lined skin. Depending on the peptide meant, it is described as either signalling skin cells to build collagen (the KTTKS/Matrixyl type) or relaxing muscle signalling (Vialox). Research so far is in cultured cells.

oligopeptide-68.summary: A brightening serum peptide that blocks tyrosinase to fade dark spots and melasma and even out skin tone.

quick.overview:
Oligopeptide-68 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide sold in serums and creams to fade dark spots and melasma and even out skin tone.

It is described in the dermatology literature as a TGF-beta1 biomimetic that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, so less pigment forms and patches fade. The human research is two small melasma studies in which it was one part of a multi-ingredient regimen, so its own contribution has not been separated out.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream, usually alongside other brightening or exfoliating ingredients and daily sunscreen. In one study it was paired with diacetyl boldine. Brightening products of this type are generally used for weeks to months.
quick.risks: The studied products also contained exfoliating acids, sunscreen filters or other depigmenting agents, so side effects cannot be attributed to the peptide alone. It is a cosmetic ingredient in the US and EU rather than a drug.

angle.text: Used in brightening serums to fade dark spots and melasma and even out tone. It is described as inhibiting tyrosinase, so less melanin forms. Human data are small melasma studies of multi-ingredient regimens.

tetrapeptide-21.summary: A four-amino-acid (GEKG) peptide in anti-aging serums for collagen support and firmer, smoother-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Tetrapeptide-21 is a short cosmetic peptide with the sequence GEKG, used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin.

Papers describe it as stimulating collagen and the extracellular matrix, the structure that gives skin its firmness. Most published work concerns getting it through the skin: a 2018 delivery study, a 2026 hydrogel study and an in vitro fibroblast study. No human clinical trial of its appearance effects was found.
quick.how: It is applied in serums and creams as part of a daily anti-aging routine. Because peptides are large, polar and easily degraded, researchers have studied enhancer molecules, carrier systems and elastin-derived hydrogels to improve delivery into skin.
quick.risks: No safety data from human trials were found. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved drug.

angle.text: Used in anti-aging serums for firmer, smoother-looking skin. It is described as stimulating collagen and matrix production in skin cells. Research so far covers skin delivery and cell-culture effects.

acetyl-tetrapeptide-3.summary: A hair-anchoring cosmetic peptide in Capixyl-type topicals for thicker, fuller-looking hair.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide used in topical products for thinning hair, and is named as the hair-anchoring ingredient in the Capixyl blend. People use it for thicker, fuller-looking hair.

It is usually combined with plant extracts such as biochanin A and ginseng. A 24-week randomized, triple-blind trial in 32 men and women with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia compared a combination of biochanin A, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 and ginseng extracts with 3% minoxidil solution. A 2026 systematic review examined peptides for hair loss in clinical trials. Because the trial tested a combination, the peptide's own effect was not isolated.
quick.how: It is applied to the scalp as a leave-on lotion or serum, typically as part of a blend and used daily. Hair-density studies run for months, as in the 24-week trial.
quick.risks: The trial listed assessing the combination's safety profile as an objective. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than an approved hair-loss drug.

angle.text: Used in scalp products for thinning hair, usually in a blend with biochanin A and ginseng, to look for thicker, fuller hair. Makers describe it as anchoring hair in the follicle so there is less shedding. A small trial tested the blend against 3% minoxidil.

palmitoyl-tetrapeptide-3.summary: A cosmetic signal peptide in serum ingredient lists, used for smoother, firmer-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-3 is a short peptide linked to a fatty chain, used in some skin-care serums for smoother, firmer-looking skin. It is grouped with the cosmetic signal peptides.

Signal peptides are generally described by manufacturers as messengers that prompt skin cells to repair and rebuild. This specific peptide appears mainly in patent filings that list it among many ingredients, combined with plant extracts and other actives. No human trials of the ingredient on its own were found, and the sources do not describe a tested mechanism for it.
quick.how: It is applied in leave-on serums and creams, always as one ingredient among several, as part of a daily anti-aging routine.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to this ingredient were found. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient rather than as an approved drug.

angle.text: Appears in serum ingredient lists as a signal peptide, where users look for smoother, firmer-looking skin. Manufacturers describe signal peptides as prompting skin repair. It is documented in patent formulations with plant extracts.

deoxyarbutin.summary: A synthetic arbutin derivative applied to fade age spots, melasma and dark patches for a more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Deoxyarbutin is a lab-made relative of arbutin used as a topical lightener to fade age spots, melasma and other dark patches and even out skin tone.

It competes with tyrosine at tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, so less pigment forms; studies describe the inhibition as reversible. A 2005 paper reported skin lightening in a pigmented guinea pig model and stronger tyrosinase inhibition than hydroquinone or arbutin in a test-tube assay. Randomized human trials were not found in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is applied as a cream or serum directly to the dark areas, typically with daily sunscreen, since sun exposure re-darkens pigment. Lightening products of this kind are used over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Researchers have compared its safety with hydroquinone in cultured cells and examined the cytotoxicity of UVB-irradiated forms. Regulatory status was not established in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Applied to fade age spots, melasma and dark patches for a more even tone. It blocks tyrosinase, so less melanin forms. Evidence comes mostly from lab and animal work.

aloesin.summary: An Aloe-derived tyrosinase inhibitor applied to lighten dark spots and even out skin tone.

quick.overview:
Aloesin is a compound from the Aloe plant used as a topical lightener for dark spots and uneven tone.

It competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, so less pigment forms, and has been reported to act synergistically with arbutin. Research is in test tubes and cells, plus a 2002 report that it inhibited UV-induced hyperpigmentation. Controlled human trials were not found.
quick.how: It is applied in lightening creams and serums, often alongside other brighteners such as arbutin and with daily sunscreen. Results from lightening ingredients build over weeks.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed give no human safety data specific to topical aloesin; most reports concern laboratory and animal models.

angle.text: Applied to lighten dark spots and uneven tone. This Aloe-derived compound inhibits tyrosinase, so less melanin forms, and is reported to work with arbutin. Evidence so far is lab-level, including a 2002 UV-pigmentation report.

ellagic-acid.summary: A fruit-and-nut polyphenol used as an antioxidant and skin brightener for a fresher, more even complexion.

quick.overview:
Ellagic acid is a polyphenol found in pomegranates, berries and walnuts, used in supplements and in some skin-care products as an antioxidant and brightener for a fresher, more even complexion.

In laboratory assays it scavenges free radicals, which is the basis for the antioxidant claim. When eaten, gut bacteria convert it into urolithins, which are absorbed better than the parent compound, and much of the research concerns these metabolites. No trial of its brightening effect on skin was found.
quick.how: It is used as a topical ingredient in brightening products and as an oral supplement or through foods such as pomegranate and berries.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports the FDA has issued warning letters to supplement companies over disease claims. No safety profile was found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Used in brightening products and supplements as an antioxidant, aiming for less dullness and a brighter complexion. It scavenges free radicals in lab assays. No skin trials of the brightening use were found.

4-n-butylresorcinol.summary: A tyrosinase inhibitor in serums that fades melasma and dark spots for a clearer, more even tone, with several small randomized trials.

quick.overview:
4-n-Butylresorcinol (butylresorcinol, rucinol) is a lab-made ingredient in serums and creams that fades melasma and age spots for a clearer, more even skin tone.

It inhibits tyrosinase and has been reported to affect tyrosinase-related protein-1, reducing melanin production in cells. It has been tested in several small randomized human trials, including split-face and vehicle-controlled designs, which reported pigment improvement versus vehicle. The trials are small and short, and head-to-head comparisons with other agents are limited.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream to pigmented areas, usually with daily sunscreen, and trial results are assessed over weeks.
quick.risks: Reports describe minimal irritation at studied concentrations. Regulation varies by country.

angle.text: Used in serums and creams to fade melasma and age spots for a more even tone. It inhibits tyrosinase, so less melanin forms. Several small randomized trials have reported improvement versus vehicle.

rhododendrol.summary: A former Japanese skin-whitening ingredient withdrawn in 2013 after users developed patchy white skin.

quick.overview:
Rhododendrol is a plant-derived melanin inhibitor that was developed to brighten skin tone in Japanese whitening cosmetics. It was used until July 2013.

It inhibits tyrosinase, but the enzyme also oxidizes it into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes, the pigment cells. Users developed patchy depigmentation (leukoderma) and the products were withdrawn. Immune involvement has also been studied. It now appears in research as a case study in depigmenting-agent safety.
quick.how: It was applied as a leave-on whitening cosmetic ingredient until its withdrawal. It is no longer sold in those products.
quick.risks: Documented harm is leukoderma. Wikipedia reports that pigment returns in most cases after stopping, and that its use has been prohibited since 2013.

angle.text: Was sold in whitening cosmetics to lighten and brighten skin by inhibiting melanin synthesis. It was withdrawn in 2013 after reports of patchy depigmentation, and is documented here as a historical product.

monobenzone.summary: A prescription depigmenting cream for extensive vitiligo that permanently removes pigment, so forums discuss it as a one-way route to paler skin.

quick.overview:
Monobenzone is a topical drug that permanently removes pigment from skin. Its approved use is in people with widespread vitiligo, where it evens out the remaining normal skin to match the depigmented patches.

In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a permanent skin whitener, with members weighing whether to go paler than their natural tone. Laboratory studies report that tyrosinase in melanocytes converts it into reactive quinones that bind cellular proteins and trigger an immune response against pigmented cells, leading to lasting loss of melanocytes. No trial has tested it for cosmetic lightening of normal skin.
quick.how: In its approved use it is a prescription cream applied to remaining pigmented skin in extensive vitiligo under medical supervision. Forum threads also describe online and gray-market purchasing for cosmetic use.
quick.risks: Reported effects include irritation, contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and depigmentation at untreated sites. The effect is described as permanent and does not reverse after stopping. It is prescription-only in the US, and use outside vitiligo is off-label.

angle.text: A prescription cream that destroys pigment cells so skin ends up uniformly pale; approved for extensive vitiligo. Forums discuss it as a permanent whitener, though use outside vitiligo is off-label and the effect is described as irreversible.

oxyresveratrol.summary: A mulberry-derived stilbene and strong tyrosinase inhibitor discussed as an ingredient for brighter, more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Oxyresveratrol is a natural compound from mulberry and related plants, discussed as a skin-brightening ingredient for dark spots and uneven tone.

Tyrosinase is the enzyme that drives melanin production, and laboratory studies on mushroom and mouse melanoma tyrosinase report potent inhibition by oxyresveratrol, which is the basis for the brightening interest. Other lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. No human trials of it for pigmentation or skin appearance were found.
quick.how: It is mentioned as an ingredient for brightening serums and creams. It is reported to be light sensitive and to degrade under UV exposure, so formulation matters.
quick.risks: No human safety data for skin use were found.

angle.text: Discussed as a brightener for dark spots and uneven tone. This mulberry-derived stilbene strongly inhibits tyrosinase in the lab, so less melanin forms. Studies so far are test-tube and animal work.

resveratrol-topical.summary: A plant antioxidant in anti-aging and brightening serums for fresher, more even-looking skin, with one 8-week trial in women over 40.

quick.overview:
Topical resveratrol is a plant polyphenol from grape skins, berries and peanuts, used in anti-aging and brightening serums for a fresher, more even look.

It is marketed as an antioxidant that limits oxidative damage to skin. Much of the published work concerns delivery: it has low water solubility and is photosensitive, and nanocarriers, emulsions and gels raise how much stays in the skin in laboratory models. An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of skin aging with trans-resveratrol, and small registered trials of resveratrol-containing products exist. Wikipedia's general resveratrol article states there is no significant evidence of an effect on aging skin.
quick.how: It is applied in serums and creams as a daily antioxidant, often with other actives and sunscreen. Formulas aim to keep it stable, since it degrades in light.
quick.risks: The sources describe no topical adverse-effect data. Reported side effects of resveratrol are mainly gastrointestinal at high oral intake. It is light sensitive and degrades easily.

angle.text: Used in anti-aging and brightening serums as an antioxidant, to limit oxidative damage and give a fresher, more even look. One 8-week trial in women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of aging; most research focuses on delivery formulations.

licochalcone-a.summary: A licorice-root compound in soothing skincare for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin, also discussed for brightening.

quick.overview:
Licochalcone A is a compound from licorice root used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin, giving calmer, clearer skin. It is also discussed for possible brightening through reduced pigment production.

Laboratory work reports antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory activity, and licorice flavonoids have been tested for tyrosinase inhibition. Human data come from acne trials of moisturizers that combine licochalcone A with other actives, so its own contribution cannot be separated.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on moisturizers and serums for redness-prone or breakout-prone skin, usually as one of several actives in a daily routine.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed give no skin safety data. Wikipedia lists generic hazard labeling for the pure chemical, which relates to handling rather than finished products.

angle.text: Used in products for sensitive, red or acne-prone skin to soothe irritation and leave skin calmer and clearer, and discussed for brightening via less pigment. Human data are acne trials of multi-ingredient moisturizers.

chitosan.summary: A shellfish-derived polysaccharide sold as a fat-binding supplement for a leaner physique and used as a carrier polymer in skincare.

quick.overview:
Chitosan is a natural polymer made from chitin in shrimp and crab shells. For appearance it shows up in two forms: an over-the-counter fat-binder supplement sold for a leaner physique, and a carrier polymer in skincare.

In the supplement, the idea is that it binds dietary fat so fewer calories are absorbed. Wikipedia reports that reviews in 2008 and 2016 found no significant effect on weight or cholesterol. In cosmetics, its amine groups become positively charged in acid, letting it form films, gels and nanoparticles that stick to tissue and carry other ingredients, for example improving skin retention of actives such as resveratrol. No human study of chitosan for skin pigmentation was found.
quick.how: Supplements are taken orally with meals, and chitosan is used as an ingredient in topical and nanoparticle formulations that deliver other actives.
quick.risks: Crustacean-derived chitosan may carry allergenic proteins, according to Grokipedia. The FDA issued a 2015 advisory about exaggerated weight-loss claims by supplement retailers.

angle.text: Sold as a fat binder so fewer calories are absorbed and the physique gets leaner, and used as a carrier polymer in cosmetics. Reviews cited by Wikipedia found no significant weight effect, and no skin-pigment effect has been shown.

diacetyl-boldine.summary: A boldo-derived brightening ingredient in serums for dark spots and melasma that stabilizes tyrosinase in its inactive form.

quick.overview:
Diacetyl boldine (DAB) is a skin-brightening ingredient derived from boldine, an alkaloid from the bark of the boldo tree. It appears in serums and creams for hyperpigmentation, dark spots and melasma, giving a more even, brighter tone.

A melasma study describes it as stabilizing tyrosinase, the enzyme that produces melanin, in its inactive form, so less pigment forms. Published human studies are few and test it inside multi-ingredient products, some compared against hydroquinone, so its effect alone has not been separated out.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream, usually as one component of a multi-ingredient brightening formula, with daily sunscreen. Pigment studies run over weeks to months.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed report no specific adverse-event data for the ingredient. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug.

angle.text: Used in serums for dark spots, hyperpigmentation and melasma, aiming for a more even, brighter tone. It is described as keeping tyrosinase in its inactive form, so less melanin forms. Studies are small combination-formula trials.

mulberry-extract.summary: A botanical skincare brightener, with mulberroside F named as the active, used for a more even-looking tone.

quick.overview:
Mulberry extract comes from Morus trees and is sold in skincare as a plant brightener for a more even, brighter-looking tone. Mulberroside F is named as the active compound.

Cosmetic marketing attributes brightening to mulberroside F, which is said to inhibit pigment production so less melanin forms. The sources reviewed do not document a mechanism in human skin, and published mulberry research concerns other uses, mainly blood glucose, antioxidant chemistry and food science. No human trial for skin tone turned up.
quick.how: It is used as an ingredient in brightening serums and creams. Mulberry fruit and leaf are also common food and supplement ingredients.
quick.risks: No skin-specific safety data were found. Mulberry fruit and leaf are common food and supplement ingredients.

angle.text: Used in skincare as a botanical brightener for a more even-looking tone. Marketing says mulberroside F reduces pigment production. Published mulberry research concerns blood sugar and antioxidants.

rice-bran-extract.summary: A K-beauty and J-beauty botanical used for brighter, smoother, moisturized skin, with antioxidant and cell-culture data behind it.

quick.overview:
Rice bran extract comes from the outer layer of milled rice and appears in Asian skincare for brightening, hydration and antioxidant effects, giving brighter, smoother skin. Rice bran and rice water have a long history of traditional use.

Constituents such as ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol, tocopherols and, in pigmented rice, anthocyanins act as antioxidants in test systems. In melanoma cells a fermented extract lowered MITF, a regulator of melanin production, and reduced melanin-pathway signalling in mouse cells. Controlled human trials for skin tone were not found.
quick.how: It is used in essences, serums, creams and cleansers, often fermented, as part of a daily brightening and moisturizing routine.
quick.risks: Safety assessments summarized by Grokipedia describe low irritation potential at typical cosmetic concentrations; that summary was not independently verified.

angle.text: Popular in K-beauty and J-beauty products for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects, for less dullness and smoother skin. Lab studies show antioxidant activity and reduced melanin signalling in mouse cells.

flutamide-topical-melasma.summary: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen tried as a 1% topical for melasma to even out facial pigmentation.

quick.overview:
Flutamide is an antiandrogen pill used for prostate cancer. A 1% topical version has been tried off-label for melasma, the facial pigmentation disorder, as an alternative to hydroquinone, to even out facial skin tone.

It blocks androgen receptors; the sources reviewed do not explain how this would affect melasma pigmentation. Wikipedia's melasma article cites a randomized trial comparing topical 1% flutamide with hydroquinone, but does not report its results.
quick.how: The topical use is a compounded cream applied to melasma patches, studied against hydroquinone. Flutamide itself is a prescription drug.
quick.risks: The oral drug carries a warning for severe liver injury and is prescription-only. No data on systemic absorption or safety of the topical form were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: An oral prostate-cancer antiandrogen studied off-label as a 1% topical for melasma, to even out facial pigmentation by blocking androgen receptors locally. One randomized comparison with hydroquinone is cited.
